result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.minimum_edge_cut()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find minimum edge cut between source and sink nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L25923-L25998){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.minimum_edge_cut( source, sink, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum edge cut](/assets/graphs/minimum-edge-cut.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two diamonds that share the hub node D, with B and E outlined as source and sink. The two accent edges B–D and C–D are the minimum edge cut separating B from E, and the card returns them as the set of pairs (B, D) and (C, D)." width="100%"} Returns the set of edges whose removal disconnects the source from the sink. Uses the max-flow min-cut theorem via Ford-Fulkerson algorithm to identify the minimum cut. For undirected graphs, edges are treated as bidirectional. For directed graphs, only forward edges are considered. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Source node (integer ID or string label). [sink]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Sink node (integer ID or string label). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [set[tuple[int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Set of edge tuples (source_id, target_id) forming the minimum cut. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or sink node doesn't exist, or if they're the same. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this diamond-shaped graph, `A` reaches `C` through two separate 2-edge paths, so breaking that connection requires removing an edge from each path: ::: {#4b569d8a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_edge("A", "B", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("B", "C", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("C", "D", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("A", "D", auto_create_nodes=True) ) # Find edges that separate A from C cut_edges = graph.minimum_edge_cut("A", "C") # Returns 2 edges, one from each of the two paths len(cut_edges) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: The same approach identifies critical links in a directed network, where redundant routers only help if all of their outgoing paths are also severed: ::: {#8f1b7b73 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_edge("Server1", "Router1", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Router1", "Router2", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Router2", "Server2", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Router1", "Router3", auto_create_nodes=True) .add_edge("Router3", "Server2", auto_create_nodes=True) ) critical_links = graph.minimum_edge_cut("Server1", "Server2") # Returns 1: the single edge from Server1 to Router1 is the bottleneck len(critical_links) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
